comment: This book is built by AI to describe distinct families and castles that share the name Rosenberg or its variations. Keep it concise and brief. Include information about each family, its members, and places related to it. Describe castles named Rosenberg in a separate section. Do not give detailed accounts of events or histories of specific people.

entries.title: Bauland and Odenwald Lords of Rosenberg

entries.english: A Franconian noble family associated with the Rosenberg near Osterburken and later centered at Boxberg. The family is attested under the Rosenberg name from the late 13th century, with an earlier tradition linking its origins to the Uissigheim ministerials. Members held Boxberg from 1381 and were connected with Wölchingen, the Schüpfergrund, Unterschüpf, Haltenbergstetten, and Bartenstein. Eberhard and Arnold appear in regional and Mainz or Palatine service, while later members included Albrecht von Rosenberg (died 1572).

entries.title: Schenk von Roßberg / Rosenberg
entries.english: The Schenk von Roßberg were a Franconian ministerial family serving the bishops of Würzburg and associated with the castle now called Schenkenschloss. The castle was known as Roßberg until around 1600; records use forms including Roßberg, Rossberg, and Rossenberg. A 1337 record names Wolfram Schenk von Rossberg, his brother Heinrich, and Heinrich's son Berthold. Other records style Schenk bearers as von Rosenberg, documenting the use of both forms in this family context.

entries.title: Mönch / Münch von Rosenberg
entries.english: The lower-noble Mönch or Münch von Rosenberg family is recorded in southwestern Germany from 1251 into the Thirty Years' War. In later centuries, its members held lands or offices connected with Mönchzell, Eberbach, Dallau, Steinsberg, and Kirchardt; some served the counts of Katzenelnbogen. Sources name Lutz, Konrad, Hans, Dieter, Ruprecht, and Peter in different periods. Prussian records also name Gerlach Mönch von Rosenberg in connection with the Teutonic Order and the Elbing region.

entries.title: Rorschach / Rosenberg of Eastern Switzerland
entries.english: The eastern Swiss knightly family known as von Rorschach and von Rosenberg served the prince-abbots of St Gallen from the 12th to the 15th centuries. Its centers and holdings included Rorschach, Herisau, Rosenberg, Rosenburg, Urstein, Berneck, and Zuckenriet. Egilolf and Rudolf appear among early members, while later records name Egli von Rosenberg at Bernang in the Rhine Valley. Branches are associated with Berneck and Zuckenriet, and some members served away from home, including in the Teutonic Order. Repeated personal names make branch identification dependent on dates, offices, and local ties.

entries.title: The South Bohemian Rožmberks
entries.english: The Witigon lords of Rožmberk, called Rosenberg in German sources and z Rožmberka in Czech, were a major house based in South Bohemia. Wok I established Rožmberk Castle after 1225 and founded Hohenfurt (Vyšší Brod) Abbey in 1259; the family later inherited the Krumlov holdings and made Český Krumlov its principal seat. Named members include Petr I and his sons Petr II, Jošt I, Oldřich I, and Jan I, followed in later generations by Ulrich II, Wilhelm, and Petr Vok, the last male-line representative. Their lands and activities also reached into the Austrian Mühlviertel. Later family tradition connected the Rožmberks with the Roman Orsini.

entries.title: Lower Austrian Lords of Rosenberg
entries.english: A local ministerial family associated with Rosenberg Castle in the Kamptal, Lower Austria. Gozwin (also written Goczwin or Godezwin) is recorded in 1175; later regional records name Konrad and Hartlieb von Rosenberg. Hans Tietze describes the castle as the seat of this ministerial family and suggests the line ended around the beginning of the 14th century. The surviving records establish the family's local setting, while its precise genealogy remains uncertain. Principal studies include Hans Tietze, Die Denkmale des politischen Bezirkes Horn in Niederösterreich (1911), p. 502; Friedrich Endl, “Die Rosenburg (bei Horn). Historisch beleuchtet” (1892), pp. 53–54; and Richard Kurt Donin, “Die Rosenburg als ein Beispiel nördlicher und südlicher Baugestaltung” (1957), p. 194.

entries.title: Rosenberg near Sulzbach: the Lengenfelders
entries.english: Records from the 14th century associate bearers styled Lengenvelder, Lengenfelder, Lengfelder, or Lengenfelderin von Rosenberg with Rosenberg near Sulzbach and nearby places. A 1343 record names Chunrad der Lengenvelder and his wife Jeute; records from 1357–1359 mention Konrad and Jeutt, their sons, and Jeutt's brother Ott, a church lord at Gebenbach. Their transactions concern places including Pfeffershoven, Oberklausen, and Sulzbach. The records document a local family group, while the relationship between its generations and similarly named bearers remains under study.

entries.title: Austrian Orsini / Ursini-Rosenberg
entries.english: A Styrian and Carinthian noble house whose medieval members used Rosenberg forms and whose later name became Ursini or Orsini-Rosenberg. Early Styrian records associate the family with Graz and styles such as de Valle, von dem Graben, and ab dem Rosenberg. In Carinthia, members held estates including Lerchenau, Mageregg, Grafenstein, Maria Loretto, Rosegg, Rottenstein, and Greifenberg. The family rose to princely rank in 1790, and the Ursini name was authorized in 1684. Family tradition included Roman ancestry and a connection with the Bohemian Rožmberks.

entries.title: Brandenburg Rosenberg bearers
entries.english: Medieval Brandenburg records name Johann and Werner Rosenberg bearers in association with the von Bredow family and with properties including Plate, Kutzkow, and Luge. A 1338 agreement places Rosenberg bearers under the protection of Markgraf Ludwig and associates them with the castle of Plate; records from 1400 name Werner and Johann as brothers in property transactions concerning Kutzkow and Luge. These sources document northern branches and their regional connections; the links among the recorded groups remain a subject for further study.

entries.subheading: Rosenberg Castle (Rosenburg am Kamp), Lower Austria
entries.english: The medieval Rosenberg in the Kamptal near Horn, Lower Austria, later became known as Rosenburg am Kamp. Monument histories describe it as a ministerial seat from the second half of the 12th century. Hans Tietze names Goczwin von Rosenberg in 1175 and Konrad subsequently; Richard Kurt Donin also cites Konrad in 1229. The castle's history is closely tied to the local Herren von Rosenberg. Key references are the European Castles Institute's EBIDAT entry for Rosenburg am Kamp; Tietze, Die Denkmale des politischen Bezirkes Horn in Niederösterreich (1911), p. 502; and Donin, “Die Rosenburg als ein Beispiel nördlicher und südlicher Baugestaltung” (1957), p. 194.

The site lies on an artificial hill at the edge of the Saale floodplain, near the river's meeting with the Elbe. In 965, Otto I granted the royal estate of Rosburch to Magdeburg's Moritzkirche; a castle is explicitly recorded as castrum Roseborg in 1269. The Counts of Barby held Rosenburg as a Magdeburg fief from 1306/08, using it for residence and administration. The medieval round fortress developed into a triangular plan, with a southern double gate and defensive enclosure; from the 1540s, residential buildings transformed it into a Renaissance seat. The palace was demolished in 1798 and largely rebuilt as an Amtshaus; the 1945 destruction left the gate tower, parts of the enclosure and vaulted cellars, later conserved. Sources: Jan Brademann, “Rosenburg (Klein-/Groß-)” in Residenzenforschung 15 (2012); Stadt Barby, Denkmalverzeichnis, entry “Burg Rosenburg”; Reinhard Schmitt, “Zur Baugeschichte des Schlosses (Amtshauses) in Klein-Rosenburg,” Burgen und Schlösser in Sachsen-Anhalt 11 (2002), pp. 155–194.

A vanished hilltop castle once stood on the Schlossberg above Rosenberg, now part of Sulzbach-Rosenberg in the Upper Palatinate. The city’s historical account dates the castle probably to around 1100 and names the Königstein ministerial family among its earliest known holders; after Ulrich II of Königstein died in 1252/53, the property passed to his son-in-law Walter Schenk von Klingenburg. In 1410 the estate became the noble Hofmark Rosenberg, later held by the Zenger von Velburg, Kemnater, Stiber, Doles, and Erlbeck families. The castle declined from the mid-16th century, and the surviving keep stump was incorporated into a war memorial inaugurated in 1929; the memorial also commemorates the dead of the Second World War. The site is a landmark above the town, with archaeological traces and views across the surrounding landscape. Sources: Stadt Sulzbach-Rosenberg Tourist-Information, ‘Schlössl und Schlossberg’; Bayerisches Landesamt für Denkmalpflege, Denkmalliste, monument D-3-71-151-172.

Rosenburg stands on a ridge above Riedenburg in the Altmühltal. Probably built in the mid-12th century, it passed to Duke Ludwig I of Bavaria in 1196 and remained with the Wittelsbach dynasty. The large complex has a Romanesque core; after destruction in 1525, Renaissance residential buildings with stepped gables shaped its present appearance. The ground-floor chapel preserves wall paintings from around 1560. The castle now houses a museum of hunting and falconry and a falconry centre. Source: Bavarian Palace Administration, “Rosenburg – Riedenburg (Altmühltal).”

Rožmberk Castle rises above the Vltava in southern Bohemia and was founded by Vok I of Rosenberg around the middle of the 13th century; the castle and Vok are documented in 1250. The complex developed as two castles, Upper and Lower. A fire in 1522 destroyed much of the Upper Castle, whose surviving landmark is the Jakobínka tower. The Lower Castle underwent Renaissance rebuilding and was later remodelled in the 19th century by the Buquoy family as a neo-Gothic family museum. Sources: National Heritage Institute of the Czech Republic, “Rožmberk”; State Archaeological List of the Czech Republic, “Rožmberk – Castle and Chateau.”

Rosenberg Fortress rises above Kronach in Upper Franconia and served as a Bamberg episcopal castle and territorial stronghold. The name is first recorded in 1249; the medieval castle was expanded through the 15th and 16th centuries, followed by bastioned fortifications that took their present pentagonal form by 1699. The fortress withstood repeated Swedish assaults during the Thirty Years’ War. After Kronach and the fortress passed to Bavaria in 1802, it lost its military status in 1867; the town acquired the site in 1888, and it now houses the Franconian Gallery and regional cultural institutions. Sources: Stadt Kronach, “Festung Rosenberg: Geschichte”; Haus der Bayerischen Geschichte, “Festung Kronach (Rosenberg)”; Historisches Unterfranken, “Burg Festung Rosenberg in Kronach.”

This vanished castle stood at Schlossplatz in Rosenberg, now part of Buchen in the Neckar-Odenwald district. Its oldest surviving feature was a keep, probably built in the 12th or 13th century; the wider castle and palace buildings are known chiefly from Tilman Ruland’s 1755 plan. The Mönch von Rosenberg are recorded as owners in 1251, followed from the late 13th century by the Lords of Rosenberg, who held the castle for more than three centuries. After the family ended in 1632, the estate passed to the Counts of Hatzfeld and, in 1730, to the Princes of Löwenstein-Wertheim-Rochefort; the palace then served as an administrative seat. The ruins were quarried for stone, and the last above-ground remains disappeared in 1926. Source: Helmut Neumaier, “Infotafel Schloss Rosenberg” (2016), Verband Odenwälder Museen; historical plan, StAWt-Rep. 5f Nr. 24, plans 2–3.
